The stinging pain snapped her back to reality. Her entire body began to tremble at the agonizingly familiar scene, a thick layer of tears blurring her vision.

Was she... reborn?

Reborn five years ago, on the day of the wedding she loathed so deeply?

She had just put on her gown when her three brothers cornered her in the bridal suite.

Because Tessa had feelings for Willow's fiancé, Elias Landon, her own brothers were forcing her to hand over the wedding. As for Asher and her other brother who hadn't arrived yet, they would undoubtedly side with Tessa without a second thought.

In her past life, when Willow refused to surrender her place at the altar, they violently stripped her out of the dress.

Ignoring her desperate pleas, they forced a spiked glass of milk down her throat.

Then, they dumped her into a stranger's bed and staged a public scandal in front of all the guests, completely destroying her reputation!

When Elias found out, he didn't even ask for an explanation. He used the opportunity to instantly break their engagement and married Tessa on the spot.

While Willow struggled frantically against the drug on a stranger's bed, Tessa walked down the aisle with Elias, wearing the custom wedding gown Willow had spent months designing.

From beginning to end, Elias never even looked at Willow once.

Later, when Tessa wanted her musical compositions, she publicly accused Willow of plagiarism. Her brothers testified for Tessa without hesitation, ruthlessly turning Willow into a stepping stone for Tessa's meteoric rise to fame.

Willow had spent three exhausting years developing a cure for Asher's illness, but her brothers simply handed the patent over to Tessa.

The list of betrayals was endless.

No matter how obedient Willow tried to be, all it took was Tessa faking a depressive episode and claiming Willow had insulted or hit her for her five brothers to throw her out of the house without a second thought.

Even when Willow produced undeniable proof that Tessa was faking it, no one believed her.

They left her to suffer a terminal illness and die alone on the streets, with no one to even claim her body.

The suffocating wave of despair from her past life crashed into her all at once, and tears spilled uncontrollably down her cheeks.

Even reliving it, the agony was entirely unbearable.

Seeing her cry, Xavier's gaze turned somber.

Though he was a powerful executive used to barking orders, he forced a patient tone to coax her into giving up her place as the bride. ""You've been pampered your whole life. You already have more than enough! It's just handing Elias over to Tessa. What is there to cry about? Enough, drink this.""

With that, he held out the glass of milk.

Willow stared at the glass. Flashes of being pinned to the bed by that terrifying stranger in her past life ripped through her mind.

It had been horrifying. Utterly suffocating.

She glared at Xavier, finally asking the question she had taken to her grave.

""I dated Elias for three years,"" she said, enunciating every single word. ""Just because Tessa said a single word, you want me to step aside. Isn't that completely ridiculous?""

Julian's usually gentle voice turned icy. ""Shouldn't you yield to Tessa? If it weren't for her parents, you'd be dead.""

Leo scolded her without an ounce of hesitation. ""How can you be so ungrateful? Tessa is an orphan because of you, and you won't even do this little thing? You're worse than a stray dog! At least a dog knows how to wag its tail when it begs!""

The barrage of accusations made Willow close her eyes. Yes, this was how it always went. Using a life debt to chain her down, slowly suffocating her until she paid with her very life, and even then, it was never enough.

She was exhausted.

Whatever she owed them, she had already paid in full.

In this life, she refused to repeat the same mistakes.

If they didn't love her, she would just have to love herself.

Willow looked up, meeting Xavier's gaze head-on. He was still gripping the glass of milk, fully determined to push her into the abyss.

Sometimes she genuinely wondered who the biological sister actually was.

She smiled. Then, raising her hand under their shocked stares, she violently swatted the glass away, sending it shattering across the floor!

Before Xavier could explode, she spoke with crystal clarity. ""Fine. I'll give up the wedding.""

Xavier's fury froze on his face. He stared at her in sheer surprise.

He had fully expected her to fight tooth and nail, having prepared countless threats to break her into submission. Yet she just agreed.

He should have been thrilled. This was exactly what he wanted. But for some inexplicable reason, a sudden wave of panic tightened his chest.

Leo eyed her warily. ""I'm going to get Tessa right now. Listen to me, Willow. You'd better not try any tricks, or I swear I won't let you get away with it!""

Willow didn't react, her eyes wandering blankly over the bridal suite's lavish decorations.

Soon, everyone except Xavier rushed out to fetch Tessa, leaving the room hollow and quiet.

Xavier watched Willow. She sat there completely still, like a lifeless doll, radiating an overwhelming sense of fragile isolation.

His heart softened slightly. After all, she was only twenty.

He lowered his voice. ""Don't blame Leo. He just wants to make things right for Tessa. You know her parents died at the hands of those kidnappers just to get you out safely. You were little and didn't understand, so I never forced you to be grateful. But you're grown now. You can't be as selfish as you used to be.""

Willow froze. Suddenly, the absolute absurdity of it all hit her.

She had been five when that kidnapping happened.

She had watched her parents get tortured to death right in front of her. She had been too terrified to even cry, and by the time she was rescued, her trauma had blocked out half her memories.

It was her brothers' painstaking care that had slowly brought her back to life.

Back then, they had genuinely loved her.

That was until she turned seven, and the Shaw family adopted Tessa.

They told Willow that she was the reason Tessa lost her parents, so it was her duty to care for Tessa and treat her like a younger sister.

Even though Tessa was actually two years older than her.

Growing up, Willow had constantly yielded out of guilt, giving up everything until she surrendered her own life.

But she was a victim too. Why did they treat her like she was the mastermind behind the tragedy?

Why did she have to pay for all the suffering in the world?

Just because she was their biological sister?

She didn't want that title anymore.

When Willow didn't respond, Xavier's momentarily gentle expression turned ice-cold again.

Stubborn as always!

And here he thought she had actually grown a conscience by stepping down!

She hadn't changed a bit!

""Tessa really likes your dress,"" Xavier ordered coldly. ""Take it off and give it to her.""

He knew she had spent over a month hand-sewing this custom gown. He knew exactly how precious it was to her.

But something this exquisite only belonged on Tessa.

Xavier braced himself for her hysterical screaming, but to his shock, she simply let out a dry laugh. ""Alright.""

Without a fuss, she turned and walked into the dressing room to strip it off.

Xavier frowned as he watched her disappear behind the door.

He hadn't expected her to surrender the dress so easily.

And he certainly never imagined that, from this very moment, she was cutting ties with the Shaw family forever.

Before entering the dressing room, Willow had discreetly scooped up a shard of glass from the shattered milk cup, carefully wrapping it and slipping it into her clutch.

It was physical proof of their attempt to drug and abuse her. She was going straight to a hospital for a toxicology screen.

She wasn't going to let today slide. Not this time!

Willow methodically removed every piece of jewelry and wiped away the bridal makeup that had taken three hours to perfect.

Half an hour later, she stared at her bare face in the mirror and offered herself a silent smile.

She turned and opened the dressing room door, running right into Tessa.

Their eyes met. Tessa's eyes were red and swollen from crying, her delicate frame trembling in a way that always made people want to protect her.

She hurried over and slumped against the doorframe in front of Willow. ""I'm so sorry. You can hit me if you want, but the thought of Elias marrying someone else just breaks my heart. It hurts so much I just want to die...""

A flash of coldness crossed Willow's eyes, but before she could speak, Leo stormed in and shoved her hard!

The brutal force slammed Willow's spine against the vanity. Blinding pain radiated through her back, stealing the breath from her lungs and leaving her dizzy.

Leo immediately supported Tessa, glaring viciously at Willow. ""Are you ever going to stop?""

Fighting through the pain, Willow grabbed the gown and jewels and hurled them right at Leo. ""Open your eyes. I didn't say a single word!""

Leo's face flushed purple with rage. ""You're getting bolder by the second! No wonder Tessa is always so terrified of you!""

Tessa hid behind Leo's broad shoulders, playing the terrified victim. Yet, when she met Willow's gaze, her beautiful eyes sparkled with undisguised triumph.

Willow stared at her coldly and scoffed. ""Say whatever you want. Since you all treat my secondhand trash like treasure, I guess I'm just feeling charitable today.""

With that, she turned on her heel to leave.

A second later, Julian's hand clamped down on her wrist.

His tone was as gentle as always, yet carried an undeniable steel. ""You can't leave yet, Willow.""

Willow glared at him as Julian's gaze flickered. ""Tessa is only an adopted daughter. Taking your place at the altar like this would look terrible. In a moment, you're going out there to publicly confess that you cheated and that you're too ashamed to face your fiancé. Then, you'll call off the wedding.""

Willow stared at him in sheer disbelief. In a heartbeat, the trap clicked into place.

Julian wanted to completely ruin her!

He wanted her to confess to infidelity and endure the wrath of the Landon family. That way, Tessa wouldn't look like a homewrecker. She would look like a saint stepping up to save the families from a humiliating scandal!

Everyone would praise Tessa's noble sacrifice while branding Willow a shameless tramp!

Based on what?

Tessa was the one stealing her fiancé, but Willow had to take the fall?

Whether she fought for the wedding or walked away, they were determined to destroy her reputation.

Willow's hands shook with fury, a hot lump forming in her throat.

Were these her brothers or her worst enemies?

Concealing her glee, Tessa feigned worry. ""Willow looks really upset. Is this too unfair to her? I... I don't mind the rumors. I've already lost everything anyway...""

Her performance tugged mercilessly at the Shaw brothers' heartstrings.

Julian's tone grew even colder. ""Are you only happy when you're making everyone else miserable, Willow?""

Willow looked up at him, a vivid memory flashing in her mind.

There was a time when Julian loved her so much. When thunderstorms terrified her, he would hold her in his arms until dawn, endlessly whispering comforts to soothe her panic.

How did they end up like this?

Swallowing the bitter lump in her throat, she offered a hollow smile. ""Fine. I'll be sensible.""

Sensible enough to never need them again.

Julian missed the absolute finality in her voice and nodded in satisfaction. Beside him, Tessa was practically vibrating with excitement as she signaled a servant.

Seconds later, a man covered in dirt and blood was dragged into the room.

A twisted satisfaction gleamed in Tessa's eyes. ""I'm so sorry, Willow. I couldn't find anyone decent on such short notice, so I had to pull a random stranger off the streets. You don't mind, do you? He's quite handsome. I think he's a perfect match for you.""

For almost two years I have not slept a full night on my own side.

Here's what it actually looks like.

I lie down on my right side, and for a little while it's fine.

Then, slowly, that hip starts to ache - a deep, heavy pressure on the outside of the joint, like someone leaning the heel of their hand into the bone and pressing harder the longer I stay there.

So I roll to my left.

Twenty minutes later, the same thing starts on that side.

Onto my back.

Stare at the ceiling.

Back to the right.

My husband started calling me a rotisserie chicken, turning over and over all night long, and the first few times I even laughed.

By about month four I wanted to throw the pillow at his head.

So I did what everyone tells you to do: I blamed the bed.

I bought a new mattress.

Hundreds of dollars, and it changed nothing.

So I figured it was the pillows - got the fancy ones, then one of those long body pillows to put between my knees.

Nothing.

I tried the topper my sister swore by.

The mattress cover that's supposed to relieve pressure points.

I even slept in the guest room for a week thinking maybe it was my side of the bed.

The ache didn't care where I slept.

Because the bed, it turns out, was never the problem.

What no one tells you about not sleeping is that it isn't only about being tired.

It's what the exhaustion does to the rest of your life.

By month six I was running on maybe three or four broken hours a night.

I'd drag myself out of bed feeling like I'd aged twenty years overnight, and it took ten minutes of shuffling around the bedroom before I could walk like a normal person.

I was short with the people I love over nothing.

I stopped making morning plans because I never knew which version of me was going to wake up.

I started dreading my own bed - lying there with a knot in my stomach, already bracing for it.

I finally went to my doctor.

She pressed on the hip, asked if it hurt here (yes) and here (god yes), nodded, and said "bursitis, common at your age - try ibuprofen and sleep on your back." I can't sleep on my back.

Two months later a different doctor called it wear and tear, gave me a cortisone shot that helped for a few weeks and then faded, and suggested maybe I just needed to lose a little weight.

Not one of them - not the GP, not the orthopedist, not anyone - asked me the question that finally explained it: when did this start, relative to my menopause?

It never occurred to me to connect the two either.

Everyone warns you about the hot flashes and the night sweats.

Nobody mentions that you'll stop being able to lie on your own side.

It's not in the menopause pamphlets.

Your friends talk about their hot flashes; nobody's talking about their hips at 3 a.m. So I never made the connection.

I finally did one of those nights I was awake anyway, scrolling to have something to do besides lie there, when I found a video from a menopause specialist.

I almost kept scrolling, because it mentioned menopause and I didn't think that had anything to do with my hip.

But I was awake anyway, so I let it play.

A couple of minutes in, she explained exactly what happens inside the hip during menopause - why the ache lands in that one specific spot on the outside of the joint, and why lying on it at night hurts the way it does.

For the first time, it made sense.

It wasn't the mattress.

It wasn't how I was sleeping.

It wasn't my age.

And it wasn't in my head.

There was a real, physical reason this was happening, and just understanding it finally made me feel like I wasn't imagining it.

She also walked through a simple routine women are using to actually get relief - not to cover it up or work around it, but to rebuild what had been quietly breaking down.

I started doing it too, and it's the first thing in two years that's let me stay on one side long enough to fall asleep.

I won't promise it's your answer.

I don't know your body.

But if you flip from hip to hip all night like a rotisserie chicken, if you've bought every mattress and pillow and none of it touched the real thing, if you've started dreading your own bed and half-wondering whether it's all in your head, give it ten minutes.

I'll leave it right below - no email, no sign-up, just press play.

She explains the why better than I could at three in the morning.

Watch it tonight, before you buy one more pillow.
headline: Why You Can't Sleep on Your Side Anymore

Do you have zero desire in perimenopause or menopause? Unfortunately, there are many reasons that libido can be poor (or disappear entirely) during the menopause transition:

* Low levels of estrogen and testosterone can affect neurotransmitters in parts of the brain that mediate sexual response

* Symptoms like poor sleep, exhaustion, and mood changes

* Sex can start to hurt because of vaginal dryness or narrowing, or pelvic floor problems

Treating low libido in menopause is not so simple as just taking hormones, though they can help! However, improving desire and overall sexual well-being and satisfaction includes managing many issues, including:

* Mental and emotional health

* Stress

* Sleep

* Communication with your partner, if you have one

* Treatment of causes of pain with sex

If you're experiencing problems with libido, pain with sex, or any other issues, please see your doctor for an evaluation, and to discuss options for treatment. You deserve to be satisfied in all aspects of your health, including sex!

text:
Let’s talk about the #Menopause questions everyone has but nobody wants to ask... Vaginal dryness, hair loss, brain fog, mood swings, low libido. 
 
If you’re searching Reddit at 2 am for answers, this DocTalk’s for you. Tune into this episode at the link in our bio! #PartnerInCare #ClinicalExpert

The molecule that ends vaginal dryness after menopause was discovered in 1934.

Your gynecologist has never once offered it to you.

It BOILS my blood, because I found it by accident after two years of pain.

I'm not going to walk you through two years of pain. You're living it. You know the burning, the dryness that made lube feel like a joke.

Let me tell you what I found the night I stopped believing I had to live with a dry vagina and painful sex — the night that made me so angry I wrote this post today.

Once you see what it really is, you'll be as angry as I am.

Your body makes one molecule whose only job is holding water in that tissue. After menopause, it drops by up to 94%.

That's it. That's the whole thing.

The vaginal tissue dries from the inside, thins, and tears at the lightest touch. That's the sandpaper. 

That's the blood on the sheets you've been blaming yourself for. Not aging. One molecule, GONE.

And here's the part that made my throat tight in anger.

That molecule isn't rare. It's called hyaluronic acid, and medicine has used it everywhere for ninety years.

Eye surgeons use it. Knee surgeons inject it. It's in the face cream on your shelf right now. Dentists use it to heal the inside of your mouth.

Everywhere on your body. Except the one place menopause was stripping it from.

Not because it was hard. The molecule was right there. They just decided that once you stopped being able to have kids, the rest of you wasn't worth the trouble. So they handed you a tube and told you to cope. 

That's when I understood why nothing I'd tried before was made to heal, and only made my symptoms worse.

For example, the lube doctors recommend only puts water on top of tissue that's dry from the inside. It's like trying to soak a waterproof jacket.

And I thought I could just use  hyaluronic acid, but that molecule is too big to be absorbed by the vaginal tissue.

That's why you need it in the lesser form: sodium hyaluronate.

And OMG, this article I read made me hold my head, because I could not believe it.

In 2023, sodium hyaluronate went head to head with a $1,500 laser treatment for vaginal dryness.

And guess what?

They both had the same result for the two groups of females… that's how POWERFUL this thing is.

And all this time no one said a word\!

A product that treats the symptom keeps you a subscription and a money machine. That's why they never hand off the thing that actually treats the tissue.

But that ends today\!

After sodium hyaluronate brings water back to the vaginal tissue, it doesn't end there.

Because your tissue is torn and you need something to build it back up, which is why you need Centella. Burn units have used it for centuries to rebuild what got thin enough to bleed.

And this is the part that scared me the most and made me anxious.

If the vaginal wall is left torn and untreated, it lets bad bacteria in, causing BV, yeast infections, and leaving us to live on antibiotics forever\!

Third, we need something to calm the burning and protect us from the infection cycle, and that's what chamomile, mallow, and tea tree oil do.

Six ingredients, every one already trusted in real medicine for centuries. They just used them on everyone but us. Burn victims got them. Cancer patients got them. 

And the whole time, the one place menopause was tearing apart got a tube of lube. 

And this is what led me to do more research, to look for a product that actually combines sodium hyaluronate and the other ingredients. 

I looked for one that's hormone-free, because cancer runs in my family. 

One gentle enough for tissue that's already raw. And reaction-free, because my hooha reacts to everything.

So I found a suppository, inserted inside the vagina to target the actual tissue.

Because I knew pills don't work — the stomach acid destroys them before they reach the tissue — and topical creams don't get absorbed.

text:
Twelve doctor appointments.

Two MRIs, one CT scan, countless X-rays.

And not a single doctor thought to ask me one simple question.

The question that would have explained everything.

The question that took me YEARS to figure out. 

========

I'm 54. And for the past three years, I've been fighting a hip pain that no one could properly diagnose. 

And honestly? I was starting to think I was losing my mind.

It started small. Just this stabbing ache on the outside of my hip after my morning walks. The kind of thing you brush off. Slept wrong. Need new shoes. Finally feeling my age.

But it didn't go away. It got worse.

The pain started waking me up at night. I'd lie on my left side and within minutes, this deep burning pressure would build.

Like someone slowly pressing their thumb into the bone, harder and harder until I couldn't take it anymore. I'd flip to my right side. Twenty minutes later, same thing. Flip again. Left side. Right side. Stare at the ceiling. Try my back. 

My husband started calling me a rotisserie chicken.

I laughed the first few times. By month four, I wanted to throw my pillow at his head.

========

Here's what no one tells you about chronic pain: 

It's not just the pain. It's everything the pain takes from you.

By month six, I was averaging maybe three hours of broken sleep. I'd drag myself out of bed feeling like I'd aged twenty years overnight — this deep stiffness that took a full ten minutes of shuffling around the bedroom before I could walk normally. 

Stairs became something I had to psych myself up for. That shooting ache down my outer thigh with every single step. I started planning my whole day around avoiding them.

I stopped going to my Thursday morning yoga class. Cancelled on my sister's birthday dinner. Skipped my nephew's soccer games because the metal bleachers were agony and standing on the sidelines wasn't much better.

I was becoming the woman who always had a reason she couldn't come.

That wasn't who I was. I used to be the one organizing things. Dragging everyone out for hikes. First one on the dance floor at weddings, last one to leave. I once walked nine miles through Rome in a single day just because I didn't want to miss anything.

Now I was the one people had learned to stop inviting.

========

And the nights... God, the nights were the worst.

I'd lie there in the dark, brain spinning out of control, convinced something was seriously wrong. Bone cancer. A tumor. Some degenerative disease quietly eating away at my hip socket while doctors kept telling me everything looked "normal." I'd catastrophize for hours while the pain pulsed and my husband slept peacefully six inches away.

One night — maybe month eight or nine, I'd stopped keeping track by then — he rolled over and put his arm around me. This thing he's done for twenty-three years of marriage. His hand rested on my hip, gentle, half-asleep.

And I flinched. Pulled away. Couldn't help it. Even that soft pressure was too much.

He didn't say anything. But I saw his face in the glow of the alarm clock.

I still think about that look.

We don't really touch anymore. Not like we used to. And I can't tell if it's because I've pulled away so many times he's stopped trying, or because I've started preemptively angling my body away from him in bed, protecting that hip like it's made of glass.

Probably both.

========

That was the week I finally went to my doctor.

She pressed on my hip, asked if it hurt here (yes), here (god yes), and here (I nearly levitated off the table). She nodded like she'd solved a puzzle.

"Bursitis. Pretty common at your age. Take ibuprofen, ice it, should calm down in a few weeks."

It didn't.

Two months later, I was back. She referred me to an orthopedist.

He squinted at my X-rays for maybe sixty seconds while I sat there in that paper gown, feeling like a specimen.

"Some arthritis. Normal wear and tear. You're what, mid-fifties?" He said it like that explained everything. "We can try cortisone if the ibuprofen isn't cutting it."

The first injection actually helped. For about three weeks, I felt almost normal. Slept on my side two nights in a row. Started making plans again.

Then it came back. Worse somehow.

Second injection lasted maybe ten days. Third one might as well have been saline.

I went to another orthopedist — paid $400 out of pocket because supposedly he was "the best." Same answer. Arthritis. Wear and tear. "Have you considered physical therapy?"

So I tried it. Twice a week for two months. Clamshells, bridges, resistance bands, stretches that were supposed to "strengthen the stabilizers."

But every night, the pain was the same. Sometimes worse — there were days after PT when I could barely make it up my front steps.

When I told my therapist it wasn't helping, she looked almost hurt. "You have to trust the process."

I stopped going after ten weeks. Couldn't justify the copays for something that wasn't working.

Here's the thing about pain that doesn't show up on tests: doctors start looking at you differently.

You can see it. The slight skepticism. The barely-hidden impatience. The unspoken suggestion that maybe you're exaggerating. 

One doctor asked if I'd "considered talking to someone." Took me a second to realize he meant a therapist.

I drove home and sat in my car in the driveway for twenty minutes, engine off, just staring at my garage door. Wondering if this was just my life now. Wondering if I really was being dramatic. Wondering if everyone was right and I just needed to accept that this is what fifty-four feels like.

Wondering how many more years of this I could actually survive.

That was my lowest point.

========

Here's what I need you to understand about those three years and twelve appointments:

Every single doctor asked me the same questions.

Where does it hurt? How long has it been going on? Does it radiate? Any numbness or tingling? What makes it worse? What makes it better? Any injuries? What's your activity level? Family history of arthritis?

They asked about my weight. My exercise habits. My stress levels. Whether I'd tried yoga. Whether I'd tried losing weight. Whether I'd tried "just resting it."

But not ONE of them — not my GP, not the orthopedists, not the physical therapist, not the rheumatologist — asked me the question that actually mattered:

When did this start relative to my menopause?

It never even occurred to me to connect the two. Why would it?

Everyone warns you about the hot flashes. The night sweats. The mood swings. The brain fog. The weight that suddenly clings to your midsection no matter what you eat.

But hip pain that feels like someone's driving a railroad spike into your outer thigh every time you try to sleep on your side?

Nobody mentions that. It's not in any of the menopause pamphlets. Your gynecologist doesn't bring it up. Your friends complain about hot flashes over wine — nobody's talking about their hips.

So I never made the connection.

Until 2:47 AM on a Tuesday.

I remember the exact time because I'd been watching the clock for hours. 

I was scrolling through my phone because sleep wasn't coming and I needed something to do besides lie there counting the ways my body had failed me.

And I found this video from a menopause researcher.

I almost kept scrolling. I'd watched dozens of videos by then. Read hundreds of articles. Tried every stretch, every supplement, every sleeping position anyone had ever suggested. None of them told me anything useful.

But something made me click. Maybe it was the 2 AM desperation. Maybe I was just too tired to keep scrolling. Maybe some part of me wasn't ready to give up yet.

Whatever it was, I'm grateful for it every single day.

Because about two minutes in, this researcher asked a question that made my whole body go still.

"Did your pain start around or after menopause?"

I paused the video.

Sat up in bed. Hip screaming at the sudden movement, but I barely noticed.

Did it?

I tried to remember. When did this really start? Not the bad pain — the early stuff. The first time I noticed something wasn't quite right.

I thought back. When did I first start waking up stiff? When did stairs first become a thing I noticed? When did I first feel that weird ache after a long walk?

And I realized: it was about eight months after my periods stopped completely. Right around the time I'd finally accepted that menopause was "over" and I could stop thinking about it.

I'd never connected those two things.

In three years of doctors and tests and failed treatments, I'd never once thought: wait. This started right after menopause. Is that a coincidence?

And nobody — not a single medical professional — had ever suggested it might not be.

I pressed play.

And what this researcher explained over the next ten minutes:

About what's actually happening inside the hip during and after menopause.

========

I'm not going to tell you this video will be your answer. I don't know your body. I don't know your situation. I don't know what's causing your specific pain.

But I know this:

If you've been fighting hip pain that doesn't show up on X-rays...

If doctors keep calling it arthritis or bursitis while the treatments don't work...

If you've started wondering whether you're just being dramatic, whether this is just "getting older," whether you should just accept it and stop complaining...

Watch this video.

It's about ten minutes. It might be the first thing about your hip pain that actually makes sense.

I'm not saying that to sell you anything. I'm saying it because I spent three years in pain when I didn't have to. Three years of my life. Three years of sleep. Three years of slowly pulling away from my husband, my friends, myself.

I don't want that for you.

Click below. Watch it tonight.

And maybe, FINALLY, you'll have the answer to the question no one thought to ask.

Vaginal Gummies are a Scam? I'm Dr. Michelle Bennett. I Created them.
Here's the Truth.

I've been awake since 4 AM reading the comments.

"I heard this is a scam."
"My friend bought a bag and nothing happened."
"These are just candy with pineapple flavoring."
"Mine were bright orange and did nothing."
"The reviews are fake."

I've read them all.
Every single one.

And instead of ignoring them like most brands do, I'm going to answer
them directly.
Because you deserve the truth.

And because the real story is stranger than you think.

My name is Dr. Michelle Bennett.
I'm a gynecologist with 20 years of clinical experience.
I spent those years watching women come into my office with the same
three complaints. The smell. The discomfort. The dryness.

And I watched almost every one of them apologize to me for it.
As if it were a discipline problem.
As if she hadn't washed enough, tried enough, cared enough.
It was never a discipline problem.
It was a product problem.

I created AllFeams.
And yes, some of what you've read about it online?
It's true.
Let me explain.

=========================================
Why People Think AllFeams Is a Scam

The first reason is simple: there are fakes.
A lot of them.

It took years and a team of formulators to get the real ingredient into a
gummy.

Not a watered-down version.
The pineapple stem extract, at a dose that does something.

And it worked.

We ran a study on 1,000 women, and 93% noticed a difference within the
first couple of weeks.
Then it was 10,000 women.
Then 100,000.

Somewhere in there it turned into 2,000 reviews on Trustpilot sitting at 4.5.

That's when the trouble started.

At first we sold it in a pink bag. The one you saw everywhere on TikTok last
year.

Factories in China copied the bag and started selling it for $10 or $20.
So we switched to the Flora+ premium golden jar.

We thought that would be the end of it.

They did it again.
Same shape. Same colors.
They lifted our photos off our own website and used them to sell it.
$30, sometimes $9.
Then they took the name.

I'm not going to name names.
But I will tell you what those copies have: sugar, pineapple flavoring, and
orange dye.
That's it.
No bromelain.
No stem extract.
No dose of anything.
It's candy with marketing.

We could have fought them one listing at a time for the rest of our lives.
Instead we did something that made no sense for a business.

We walked away from our own name.
Every review, every video, every search that led to us. Gone.

Because the name had stopped meaning us.
It meant whatever was in the cheapest bag that week.

So now we're AllFeams.

And we added something they will never bother to copy.
I'll get to that.

When someone buys a bag for $9, takes it every day for a month, sees
nothing, and writes "AllFeams is a scam," she's right about the experience.

But she was never taking AllFeams.
The original is not sold on Amazon.
Not on eBay.
Not on TikTok Shop.
Not in stores.
It is exclusively available through our official website, in the golden jar, with
bromelain from the stem printed on the label.

But here's the harder part of the answer.
The one most brands never say.
============================================================
===
Even the Real AllFeams Doesn't Work for Everyone. Here's Why.
I said this once in an interview and got attacked for it.

People said I was "admitting my product doesn't work."
No.
I was admitting something the feminine care industry will never say out
loud:

The smell, the discomfort, and the dryness are not a hygiene problem.
They're an internal problem.

And if you treat an internal problem with a surface solution, you will get
nothing.

Let me explain what I mean, because this is the part that changes
everything.
Your body is supposed to manage this on its own.

A population of protective bacteria keeps the pH where it belongs, keeps
the tissue comfortable, and keeps you smelling like nothing at all.
When that population gets pushed out, the bacteria that take over do
something clever.
They build a film.

A layer that shields them from everything you throw at them from the
outside.
Washes can't reach it.
They strip the surface, including the protective bacteria you had left, and
the smell comes back stronger.
I've watched women scrub their way into a worse problem for years.
Wipes and sprays cover it for an afternoon.
Boric acid and the treatments your doctor prescribes clear the surface
population, and they should.
If your doctor gave you something, take it.
What they don't reach is the film underneath.
So the problem waits.
And it comes back.

And a gummy that's sugar, flavoring, and dye never gets anywhere near any
of this.
That is why I spent years building something different.

=====================================================
The Three Things the Copies Can't Replicate

What I needed was a way to reach the film.
From the inside out.
At home.
Without another appointment, another course of something, another bottle
to wash with.

THE FIRST: The stem, not the fruit.
The whole reason these gummies work has nothing to do with pineapple
fruit.
It's an enzyme called bromelain, and it comes from the stem of the plant.
The fruit gives you the taste and the smell.
The stem gives you the enzyme that breaks down the film these bacteria
hide behind.
This is enzyme chemistry, not a TikTok trend.
Have you ever seen an orange pineapple?
If your gummies are bright orange instead of golden yellow, that's dye, not
enzyme.
And if the bag promises to make you smell like pineapple, that bag has
never met bromelain.
Real bromelain doesn't make you smell like anything.
It works on what's making the smell, so you smell normal and like yourself
again.

THE SECOND: A dose that does something.
This is the thing they will never bother to copy.
The copies have zero bromelain.
Not a small amount. Zero.
The real one has the full dose of stem extract, packed into a jar that's full
to the lid, not a bag that's seventy percent air.
That's where the money goes.

Not into the bag.
Into the gummy.

THE THIRD: Time.
This is the part the people selling the copies will never tell you.
If you want this to work overnight, don't buy it.
It's rebuilding something that took years to come apart, so it works over
weeks, not hours.
Most women notice something within the first couple of weeks.
The women who get somewhere are the ones who stay on it.
Because once the film is gone, your body relearns how to keep itself fresh,
comfortable, and in balance on its own.

Stem. Dose. Time.

That's what took years to get into a gummy.
That's what the $9 bag cannot replicate with flavoring.
===============================================
The Women Who Decided It Was Their Body

Every week we get a version of the same message.
The details change. The story doesn't.
Here's what it sounds like.

She's a lawyer in her fifties.

She reads fine print for a living. She did not read the label.

For most of the last few years she'd been carrying wipes in her handbag
and a spare pair of underwear in her desk drawer.

She showered before bed and again in the morning, and by lunch she was
checking anyway.

The dryness she'd stopped mentioning to anyone, including her husband,
who'd stopped asking.

She'd been to two gynecologists. Both told her everything looked normal.

Then she saw the pink bag on TikTok.
Searched the name.
Bought two bags of the copy. $30 each. $60 for two months.
Bright orange. Tasted like candy.
She took them every day for two months.

Nothing.

So she did what most women do.
She decided it was her body.
That this was just her fifties now, and she'd better get used to it.

A friend from her firm sent her the real one.

She assumed it was probably a scam, or a very good one.

She took them anyway, mostly to prove her friend wrong.

Within the first couple of weeks, she stopped checking at lunch.
The wipes were still in her handbag. She just hadn't used them.
Then she stopped rehearsing excuses at bedtime.

The message usually ends with something like this:
"I read contracts all day and I bought a zip-lock bag of orange candy
because the video was convincing and it was $30. I'd already decided it
was my age. Then I took the real one. I stopped carrying wipes. I stopped
making excuses at night. My husband said I smell like me again. Not like
pineapple. Like me. I threw the bags away. I kept the jar."

She is not an outlier.

In our study of 1,000 women:

text:
Why Copper Vanished from Medicine 🔶

Most people think copper jewelry is a folk remedy.

Something grandmothers believed in.

Something without real science behind it.

They're wrong.

In the 1800s, physicians across America and Europe were prescribing copper bracelets to their patients as standard practice — not as an alternative treatment, but as medicine.

The reason was simple.

Copper destroys bacteria, fungi and pathogens on contact.

Scientists called it the oligodynamic effect.

Hospitals knew it.

Physicians relied on it.

Patients wore copper daily.

But the benefits went deeper than anyone expected. 🧬

The human body runs on electricity.

Every heartbeat is a frequency.

Every nerve impulse is a signal.

When copper sits directly against skin, something remarkable happens — the body begins to absorb its charge.

Oxidative stress neutralizes.

Internal systems recalibrate.

Circulation responds.

Patients who wore copper recovered faster than those who didn't.

Doctors had no explanation.

They just knew it worked. ⚡️

So why did it disappear?

The answer is exactly what you'd expect.

As pharmaceutical interests took over medical education in the early 1900s, the entire model of medicine shifted — from prevention and passive healing, to perpetual treatment.

A patient who heals themselves is not a customer.

Copper had no patent.

No profit margin.

No place in the new system.

So it was quietly removed.

Replaced.

Forgotten. 👀

But not entirely.

Because one woman kept making it.

Her name is Vera.

She's 69, she lives in Sedona, and she's been hammering copper by hand since 1984 — long before any of this became a trend.

She's not a brand.

She's just been doing this her whole life.

You can't see it, but her fountain could be growing the number-one bacteria behind cat UTIs.

And most cat parents have no idea.

Researchers found litter-box bacteria, E. coli included, in 2 out of 3 cats' water bowls.

A recirculating fountain pushes that water through a warm pump for days. And E. coli, the number-one bacteria behind cat UTIs, breeds in it. 🦠

So you trust the filter.

But a filter is for hair, odour and taste. The makers say so themselves, and not one says bacteria. It sits wet in the loop for two weeks, and wet carbon is where bacteria breed.

The pink slime that keeps coming back is the tell-tale sign.

So you upgrade to stainless steel, because vets recommend it.

But the bowl was never the problem. The loop is. The water in that steel bowl still goes round through a plastic pump for days. New bowl. Same old water.

And that water doesn't stay in the bowl. The E. coli ends up in her bladder and kidneys. That's where a UTI begins.

A UTI visit runs $150 to $400. Untreated, it climbs to her kidneys: $2,500 to $5,000, and it can kill her.

She drinks for a minute at a time. You never see it happen.

So why has no one fixed it?

$40 for the fountain. $1,100 in filters. A fountain that doesn't loop wouldn't need a filter. So in thirty years they changed the bowl three times and the loop never once.

The filter is the business model. Her water isn't.

They never built a fountain without the loop. So we did. 💧

PureStream is the first loop-free cat fountain. Two sealed tanks. Every 6, 9 or 12 hours the steel tray dumps the used water into the waste tank and refills from the clean side.

The old water never comes back. And E. coli never gets the days it needs to grow.

text:
The moment I started questioning if I was in perimenopause wasn't a hot flash. It wasn't my period. It was my skin. 🪞

I partnered with @midihealth to tell this story because it's the most honest one I have. Hormonal acne was my first sign — breakouts on my jaw and chin that I couldn't explain, texture and tone that kept shifting. And the strangest part? Everything showed up on my skin. What I ate, how I slept, my mood, my hormones — it all wrote itself onto my face.

Turns out this is incredibly common in perimenopause. As estrogen shifts, it changes oil production, inflammation, and how resilient your skin barrier is — so your skin isn't overreacting, it's responding to something real happening underneath.

That's what led me to Midi Health — a virtual care platform built around hormone health, offering prescription-strength skincare prescribed by a Midi clinician based on what your skin actually needs, not something you'd pick up over the counter. Midi skincare products require a Midi clinician visit or a qualifying questionnaire to receive a prescription.

I'm booking my own Midi visit to get some real answers — documenting the whole process as I go.

Midi is covered by most major insurance (copay/deductible may still apply), and self-pay is always an option.

Individual experience shown. Results may vary. Images unedited.

Book your visit: link in bio or Comment "MIDI" and I'll send the link straight to your DMs.

#MidiHealthPartner

Husbands, you may not hear it, you may not notice it, but that doesn’t mean that your wife isn’t struggling to sleep in perimenopause and menopause. Twelve doctor appointments.

Two MRIs, one CT scan, countless X-rays.

And not a single doctor thought to ask me one simple question.

The question that would have explained everything.

The question that took me YEARS to figure out. 

========

I'm 54. And for the past three years, I've been fighting a hip pain that no one could properly diagnose. 

And honestly? I was starting to think I was losing my mind.

It started small. Just this stabbing ache on the outside of my hip after my morning walks. The kind of thing you brush off. Slept wrong. Need new shoes. Finally feeling my age.

But it didn't go away. It got worse.

The pain started waking me up at night. I'd lie on my left side and within minutes, this deep burning pressure would build.

Like someone slowly pressing their thumb into the bone, harder and harder until I couldn't take it anymore. I'd flip to my right side. Twenty minutes later, same thing. Flip again. Left side. Right side. Stare at the ceiling. Try my back. 

My husband started calling me a rotisserie chicken.

I laughed the first few times. By month four, I wanted to throw my pillow at his head.

========

Here's what no one tells you about chronic pain: 

It's not just the pain. It's everything the pain takes from you.

By month six, I was averaging maybe three hours of broken sleep. I'd drag myself out of bed feeling like I'd aged twenty years overnight — this deep stiffness that took a full ten minutes of shuffling around the bedroom before I could walk normally. 

Stairs became something I had to psych myself up for. That shooting ache down my outer thigh with every single step. I started planning my whole day around avoiding them.

I stopped going to my Thursday morning yoga class. Cancelled on my sister's birthday dinner. Skipped my nephew's soccer games because the metal bleachers were agony and standing on the sidelines wasn't much better.

I was becoming the woman who always had a reason she couldn't come.

That wasn't who I was. I used to be the one organizing things. Dragging everyone out for hikes. First one on the dance floor at weddings, last one to leave. I once walked nine miles through Rome in a single day just because I didn't want to miss anything.

Now I was the one people had learned to stop inviting.

========

And the nights... God, the nights were the worst.

I'd lie there in the dark, brain spinning out of control, convinced something was seriously wrong. Bone cancer. A tumor. Some degenerative disease quietly eating away at my hip socket while doctors kept telling me everything looked "normal." I'd catastrophize for hours while the pain pulsed and my husband slept peacefully six inches away.

One night — maybe month eight or nine, I'd stopped keeping track by then — he rolled over and put his arm around me. This thing he's done for twenty-three years of marriage. His hand rested on my hip, gentle, half-asleep.

And I flinched. Pulled away. Couldn't help it. Even that soft pressure was too much.

He didn't say anything. But I saw his face in the glow of the alarm clock.

I still think about that look.

We don't really touch anymore. Not like we used to. And I can't tell if it's because I've pulled away so many times he's stopped trying, or because I've started preemptively angling my body away from him in bed, protecting that hip like it's made of glass.

Probably both.

========

That was the week I finally went to my doctor.

She pressed on my hip, asked if it hurt here (yes), here (god yes), and here (I nearly levitated off the table). She nodded like she'd solved a puzzle.

"Bursitis. Pretty common at your age. Take ibuprofen, ice it, should calm down in a few weeks."

It didn't.

Two months later, I was back. She referred me to an orthopedist.

He squinted at my X-rays for maybe sixty seconds while I sat there in that paper gown, feeling like a specimen.

"Some arthritis. Normal wear and tear. You're what, mid-fifties?" He said it like that explained everything. "We can try cortisone if the ibuprofen isn't cutting it."

The first injection actually helped. For about three weeks, I felt almost normal. Slept on my side two nights in a row. Started making plans again.

Then it came back. Worse somehow.

Second injection lasted maybe ten days. Third one might as well have been saline.

I went to another orthopedist — paid $400 out of pocket because supposedly he was "the best." Same answer. Arthritis. Wear and tear. "Have you considered physical therapy?"

So I tried it. Twice a week for two months. Clamshells, bridges, resistance bands, stretches that were supposed to "strengthen the stabilizers."

But every night, the pain was the same. Sometimes worse — there were days after PT when I could barely make it up my front steps.

When I told my therapist it wasn't helping, she looked almost hurt. "You have to trust the process."

I stopped going after ten weeks. Couldn't justify the copays for something that wasn't working.

Here's the thing about pain that doesn't show up on tests: doctors start looking at you differently.

You can see it. The slight skepticism. The barely-hidden impatience. The unspoken suggestion that maybe you're exaggerating. 

One doctor asked if I'd "considered talking to someone." Took me a second to realize he meant a therapist.

I drove home and sat in my car in the driveway for twenty minutes, engine off, just staring at my garage door. Wondering if this was just my life now. Wondering if I really was being dramatic. Wondering if everyone was right and I just needed to accept that this is what fifty-four feels like.

Wondering how many more years of this I could actually survive.

That was my lowest point.

========

Here's what I need you to understand about those three years and twelve appointments:

Every single doctor asked me the same questions.

Where does it hurt? How long has it been going on? Does it radiate? Any numbness or tingling? What makes it worse? What makes it better? Any injuries? What's your activity level? Family history of arthritis?

They asked about my weight. My exercise habits. My stress levels. Whether I'd tried yoga. Whether I'd tried losing weight. Whether I'd tried "just resting it."

But not ONE of them — not my GP, not the orthopedists, not the physical therapist, not the rheumatologist — asked me the question that actually mattered:

When did this start relative to my menopause?

It never even occurred to me to connect the two. Why would it?

Everyone warns you about the hot flashes. The night sweats. The mood swings. The brain fog. The weight that suddenly clings to your midsection no matter what you eat.

But hip pain that feels like someone's driving a railroad spike into your outer thigh every time you try to sleep on your side?

Nobody mentions that. It's not in any of the menopause pamphlets. Your gynecologist doesn't bring it up. Your friends complain about hot flashes over wine — nobody's talking about their hips.

So I never made the connection.

Until 2:47 AM on a Tuesday.

I remember the exact time because I'd been watching the clock for hours. 

I was scrolling through my phone because sleep wasn't coming and I needed something to do besides lie there counting the ways my body had failed me.

And I found this video from a menopause researcher.

I almost kept scrolling. I'd watched dozens of videos by then. Read hundreds of articles. Tried every stretch, every supplement, every sleeping position anyone had ever suggested. None of them told me anything useful.

But something made me click. Maybe it was the 2 AM desperation. Maybe I was just too tired to keep scrolling. Maybe some part of me wasn't ready to give up yet.

Whatever it was, I'm grateful for it every single day.

Because about two minutes in, this researcher asked a question that made my whole body go still.

"Did your pain start around or after menopause?"

I paused the video.

Sat up in bed. Hip screaming at the sudden movement, but I barely noticed.

Did it?

I tried to remember. When did this really start? Not the bad pain — the early stuff. The first time I noticed something wasn't quite right.

I thought back. When did I first start waking up stiff? When did stairs first become a thing I noticed? When did I first feel that weird ache after a long walk?

And I realized: it was about eight months after my periods stopped completely. Right around the time I'd finally accepted that menopause was "over" and I could stop thinking about it.

I'd never connected those two things.

In three years of doctors and tests and failed treatments, I'd never once thought: wait. This started right after menopause. Is that a coincidence?

And nobody — not a single medical professional — had ever suggested it might not be.

I pressed play.

And what this researcher explained over the next ten minutes:

About what's actually happening inside the hip during and after menopause.

========

I'm not going to tell you this video will be your answer. I don't know your body. I don't know your situation. I don't know what's causing your specific pain.

But I know this:

If you've been fighting hip pain that doesn't show up on X-rays...

If doctors keep calling it arthritis or bursitis while the treatments don't work...

If you've started wondering whether you're just being dramatic, whether this is just "getting older," whether you should just accept it and stop complaining...

Watch this video.

It's about ten minutes. It might be the first thing about your hip pain that actually makes sense.

I'm not saying that to sell you anything. I'm saying it because I spent three years in pain when I didn't have to. Three years of my life. Three years of sleep. Three years of slowly pulling away from my husband, my friends, myself.

I don't want that for you.

Click below. Watch it tonight.

And maybe, FINALLY, you'll have the answer to the question no one thought to ask.
